searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: This week's lab will cover the following:  Gathering the necessary materials to run this course: External hard driveWindows Server 2025 ISOWindows 11 ISO Establishing a networking scheme for our virtual machinesUsing KVM to replicate physical network with a virtual one

searchDocs.title: Lab 1 Notes​
searchDocs.content: Lab 1 is a preparation lab and should not take you long but it MUST be completed before you can begin Lab 2.  If you have not already done so, please make sure you read through the entire MST100 Welcome Page so that you understand how this course is run.  Once you have done so, proceed with this lab.

searchDocs.title: Objectives​
searchDocs.content: By the end of this lab, you will be able to:  Acquire Windows Server 2025 Datacenter and Windows 11 Education installation media and your individual product key from Azure Education and store them securely.Access VMware Workstation on a Seneca Lab PC (or install it on a personal PC).Establish a networking scheme for your virtual machines

searchDocs.title: Investigation 1: Downloading Installation Media​
searchDocs.content: In this investigation, you will download both ISOs required to install all our virtual machines for this course, along with serial keys assigned to your Seneca username.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Windows Server 2025 Datacenter​
searchDocs.content: In this part, you will be downloading your Windows Server OS installation media by logging into your Seneca-based Azure account. You will also generate your personal serial keys for your copy of Server.  Navigate to the Microsoft Azure site: Microsoft Azure PortalUse your Seneca e-mail address and password to login.Once on the main Azure page, look for the Search bar at the top of the page.In the Search bar, type: Education, then hit Enter.In the Education | Overview page, look to the left. You will see menu items already displayed on screen. (Overview, Learning resources, etc.)Inside Learning resources in the left menu, click on Software.In the main Software page, there is a Search bar just below the word Software (it says "Search" inside it.)In that search field, type and enter: Windows Server 2025 DatacenterIn the item that appears below (there should only be one), click the link for Windows Server 2025 Datacenter.On the right, an information box appears describing the software. Using your mouse to hover over this information box, scroll down to the bottom.You should now see two items: View Key and DownloadClick on Download first to begin downloading the Server 2025 ISO. You will need this for your operating system installation. (Don't forget where you've saved it!)While the ISO file is downloading, click on View Key.Copy this key into a text file that you save locally on your computer. You will need this for the Server installation and for any reinstalls later in the semester. DO NOT FORGET WHERE YOU SAVED THIS. We will be moving it to a secure location shortly.

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Windows 11 Education​
searchDocs.content: This part is similar to Part 1. We'll follow many of the same steps and download a copy of Windows 11 instead.  Log back into the Microsoft Azure website.Go to: Education > Learning Resources > SoftwareIn the search field, type and enter: Windows 11 EducationDownload the ISO.Click on View Key to save your Windows 11 Education serial key in a secure text file.Reminder: Always store all serial keys in a secure location only you have access to.  Do not lose this key and do NOT share it with anyone!

searchDocs.title: Part 3: Creating Your MST100 Working Directories and Storing the ISOs Inside​
searchDocs.content: Now that we have our ISOs we are going to store them on our external hard drive so that we can use them to create our virtual machines in Lab 2. Before we actually move them, we are going to create a nice, organized directory structure for all of our MST100 lab work.  Plug your external hard drive into the computer you downloaded your ISOs onto and open the File Explorer.Navigate to your external hard drive.Create a directory called "MST100" and move into that directory.Inside the MST100 directory create the following 5 directories:  "ISOs""Notes""Server1""Server2""Client1"  Finally, find the Windows Server 2025 Datacenter and Windows 11 Education ISOs on your computer (probably in your Downloads directory) and copy them into your newly created "ISOs" directory.Find the text file that has your Windows security key in it and copy it into the "Notes" directory on your external hard drive.  DO NOT LOSE THIS KEY. DO NOT SHARE THIS KEY WITH ANYONE. You may want to also store a copy of this key in your OneDrive just in case your hard drive is rendered unusable.  Now you have your ISOs and security key in the right place and you have your directories ready to install to in next week's lab.

searchDocs.title: Lab 2 Notes​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: The primary method to do the labs in MST100 is to use virtual machines running on VMware inside the Seneca PC Windows image. There will be a few times in this course where you will need to have two VMs turned on at once but for the most part it is best to make sure that you have only one turned on at a time so as to ensure the stability of your system. Even so, you may experience VM crashes or system lock ups from time to time as MS Windows and VMware are quite resource intensive.  Maybe make a note on backups??

searchDocs.title: Investigation 1: Installing your VMs​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: In this investigation, you will install all 3 virutual machines using VMWare Workstation Pro on a Seneca lab computer.  Begin by logging into a Seneca lab computer and then plugging in your external hard drive (which should have your ISO files and Keys text file on it from Lab 1)Check to make sure your external hard drive is recognized by the computer by opening the File Explorer and navigating to your external hard drive.Double check that the directories you created in lab 1 are there.Open VMWare Workstation Pro from the desktop.

searchDocs.title: Part 1-1: Installing Windows Server 2025 Datacenter (GUI)​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: In this part, you will install Windows Server 2025 Datacenter with a GUI.  Click "Create a New Virtual Machine" on the Home tab in VMWare Workstation Pro.Select "Typical" and click "Next".Select "Installer disc image file (iso)" and then click "Browse".Navigate to the ISOs directory on your external hard drive and open the Windows Server 2025 ISO.You should notice a message below the path to the ISO that says "Windows Server 2025 detected. This operating system will use Easy Install". Click "Next"Enter your Windows Server 2025 product key (which should be in your "Keys" file on your external hard drive).For "Version of Windows to Install" leave the default (should be "Windows Server 2025 Datacenter").For "Full name", enter "Administrator".For "Password", enter "P@ssw0rd".Do NOT check "Log on automatically". Click "Next".For "Virtual Machine name", enter "Server1".For "Location", click "Browse" and navigate to and select the directory called "Server1" in your external hard drive and click "OK". Confirm the path to your "Server1" directory has been selected (this is important, if you create your VM on the lab computer and not your external hard drive, it will be lost when you turn off the computer). Click "Next".Leave the disk size at 60 GB and select "Store virtual disk as a single file". Click "Next"Click "Customize Hardware".Change "Memory" to 4096 MB.Change "Processors" to 1 Processor and 4 cores per processor. Click "Close". Click "Finish".The virtual machine will launch and the installation will begin. You will be asked to put your product key in once again. Do so and click "Next". *to "paste" into the VM, click inside the Product Key box so that the cursor is seen inside it, then click "Edit" in VMWare and select "Paste". From here, most of the installation will be automatic. The VM will restart several times during the installation.Eventually you will land on the Windows Server 2025 desktop and VMWare Tools will auto-install. When it is finished, it will ask you to restart the system. Click "Yes" and your VM will reboot.

searchDocs.title: Part 1-2: Windows Server 2025 GUI Post-Installation Tasks​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: Now that our Server1 is installed, there are a few things we need to do to prepare it for our labs. We are going to ensure our Time Zone is correct and we are going to name our system appropriately. Then we are going to make sure our system is completely updated. FInally, we will confirm internet connectivity and download a better web browser.  Log into your Server1. To use Ctrl+Alt+Del in your VM, click "VM" in VMware and select "Send Ctrl+Alt+Del".You should be met with the Server Manager Dashboard. If not, click on the Server Manager icon at the bottom of the screen.A pop up will appear asking you to "Try Windows Admin Center/ Azure Arc". Click "Don't show me this message again" and close the pop-up.Click "Local Server" on the left side of the screen.In the "Properties" window, look for "Time Zone" and make sure it is set to "UTC -05:00 Eastern Time". If it is something else, change it to our time zone.Next, click on the semi-randomized name next to "Computer Name". Then click "Change".Change the computer name to "S1-SenecaID" (for example, my Seneca ID is hheim so my Server1 computer name would be "S1-hheim").Leave the default Workgroup selected and click "OK". A message will pop up saying the computer name will not change until the system is restarted. Click "OK".Close the Computer Name window and another message will pop up asking if you want to restart the computer now. Click "Restart Later".Next, find "Windows Update" in the "Properties" window and click the blue text beside it. Click the blue "Check for updates" button.Windows Server will now download and install all necessary updates.While they are downloading, scroll down and click on "Advanced Options".Turn the "Receive updates to other Microsoft products" toggle from Off to On.Click "Windows Update" at the top of the screen to get back to the main Updates window.You will likely need to wait a little while for the updates to finish downloading and installing. Eventually, all the updates listed will say "Pending restart". Once you see this, click the blue "Restart now" button.Server1 will reboot and install updates. This will likely take a while and it will likely reboot a few times but just let it do its thing. Do not turn off the VM while it is updating. If your VM freezes during the updates, check with you teacher before moving forward.When you are met with the login screen, log in and return to the Updates window.Click the blue "Check for updates" button. If any remaining updates are available they will install. Repeat this cycle until you are met with a "You're up to date" message.Next, we are going to confirm internet connectivity and download a different web browser that MS Edge.Open MS Edge (the icon will be at the bottom of your screen).Go through the first-run questions (just say no to everything).Go to the Mozilla Firefox website: www.firefox.comDownload Firefox and install it.Once it is installed, open Firefox and go to google.com to make sure everything is working.Shut down Server1.  Note: During installations it is a good idea to only have one VM (the one you are installing) powered on at a time.

searchDocs.title: Part 2-1: Installing Windows Server 2025 Core (No GUI)​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: Now we are going to install our second server, Server2. This installation will be very similar to the first, although the server will look quite different when we are done.  Click "Create a New Virtual Machine" on the Home tab in VMWare Workstation Pro.Select "Typical" and click "Next".Select "Installer disc image file (iso)" and then click "Browse".Navigate to the ISOs directory on your external hard drive and open the Windows Server 2025 ISO.You should notice a message below the path to the ISO that says "Windows Server 2025 detected. This operating system will use Easy Install". Click "Next"Enter your Windows Server 2025 product key (which should be in your "Keys" file on your external hard drive).For "Version of Windows to Install" change it to "Windows Server 2025 Datacenter Core". VERY IMPORTANT!!For "Full name", enter "Administrator".For "Password", enter "P@ssw0rd".Do NOT check "Log on automatically". Click "Next".For "Virtual Machine name", enter "Server2".For "Location", click "Browse" and navigate to and select the directory called "Server2" in your external hard drive and click "OK". Confirm the path to your "Server2" directory has been selected (this is important, if you create your VM on the lab computer and not your external hard drive, it will be lost when you turn off the computer). Click "Next".Leave the disk size at 60 GB and select "Store virtual disk as a single file". Click "Next"Click "Customize Hardware".Change "Memory" to 4096 MB.Change "Processors" to 1 Processor and 4 cores per processor. Click "Close". Click "Finish".The virtual machine will launch and the installation will begin. You will be asked to put your product key in once again. Do so and click "Next". *to "paste" into the VM, click inside the Product Key box so that the cursor is seen inside it, then click "Edit" in VMWare and select "Paste". From here, most of the installation will be automatic. The VM will restart several times during the installation.Eventually you will land on the Windows Server 2025 Core config screen and VMWare Tools will auto-install. When it is finished, it will ask you to restart the system. Click "Yes" and your VM will reboot.

searchDocs.title: Part 2-2: Windows Server 2025 Core Post-Installation Tasks​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: Now that Server2 is installed we are going to perform the same post-installation tasks that we did on Server1. However, because this is the "Core" version of Windows Server 2025 there is no GUI and so our configurations will be done a little differently.  Begin by logging into Server2 (again, click "VM" in VMWare and then select "Send Ctrl+Alt+Del").Put in your password and you will be brought to the SConfig screen. SConfig is a module that allows us to make basic system configurations without the need for commands or a GUI.Find the option for "Date and Time", enter the corresponding number, and press "Enter". The Date and Time window should appear.Check to ensure that UTC -05:00 Eastern Time is selected. If not change it to that time zone. Press "OK".Next we will change the computer name. Find the option for "Computer Name", enter the corresponding number, and press "Enter".Type in your computer name as "S2-SenecaID" (for example, my Seneca ID is hheim so my Server2 computer name would be "S2-hheim").The system will ask you to restart. Select "(Y)es".Once the system reboots and you have logged back in to the SConfig screen, find the option for "Update Settings", enter the corresponding number, and press "Enter".On the "Update Settings" screen, enter "5" (Opt-in to Microsoft Update) and press "Enter". Press "Y" and press "Enter" on the next screen to confirm. Press "Enter" to continue.Back on the SConfig screen, find the option for "Install Updates", enter the corresponding number, and press "Enter".Enter "1" (All quality updates) and press "Enter".Windows Server will search for applicable updates and eventually it will ask you which updates to install. Enter "A" (All Updates) and press "Enter".Windows Server will not download and install its updates. This may take a while.Once the installations are complete, the system will ask you to restart. Enter "Y" (yes) and press "Enter".Server2 will restart. It may continue updating and restart again.When Server2 comes back up, log in and go back into the "Install Updates" option. Once again, Enter "1" and press "Enter".If there are any remaining updates, enter "Y" and press "Enter". Then, reboot if asked to.Repeat these steps until searching for all quality updates results in the "There are no applicable updates" message. Press "Enter" to return to the SConfig screen.Shut down Server2.

searchDocs.title: Part 3-1: Installing Windows 11 Education​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: In this part we are going to install our Client1 system which will be running Windows 11 Education. Unfortunately, Windows 11 does not have an Easy Install feature in VMWare so this installation will be a little more involved.  Click "Create a New Virtual Machine" on the Home tab in VMWare Workstation Pro.Select "Typical" and click "Next".Select "Installer disc image file (iso)" and then click "Browse".Navigate to the ISOs directory on your external hard drive and open the Windows 11 ISO.You should notice a message below the path to the ISO that says "Windows 11 x64 detected. Click "Next"For "Virtual Machine name", enter "Client1".For "Location", click "Browse" and navigate to and select the directory called "Client1" in your external hard drive and click "OK". Confirm the path to your "Client1" directory has been selected (this is important, if you create your VM on the lab computer and not your external hard drive, it will be lost when you turn off the computer). Click "Next".Windows 11 uses TPM hardware to encrypt certain important files. VMware Worksation adds the TPM module automatically as long as you select the right options:  Choose Encryption Type: Only the files needed to support a TPM are encrypted.Password: Your normal VM password.  Click "Next".Leave the disk size at 64 GB and select "Store virtual disk as a single file". Click "Next"Click "Customize Hardware".Change "Processors" to 1 Processor and 4 cores per processor. Click "Close". Click "Finish".When the VM starts, pay close attention to the black screen. As soon as you see the "Press any key..." message, click with your mouse into the VM and press the space bar. Failure to do so will result in the VM not booting to its installer and you will have to begin again.On the "language setting" screen, use the default selections and click "Next".On the "keyboard setting" screen, use the default selections and click "Next".On the "setup option" screen, select "Install Windows 11", check the "I agree everything..." box and click "Next".On the next screen, enter your Product Key for Windows 11 (this will be a different key than the Windows Server key) and click "Next".Accept the license terms on the next screen.On the "location to install" screen, select the only available option and click "Next".On the "Ready to install" screen, click "Install".Windows 11 will now install. It will reboot and take some time before you arrive at the next input screen.When you regain control you will be on the "country or region screen". Select "Canada" and click "Yes".On the "keyboard layout" screen, leave the default ("US") and click "Yes".Skip a second keyboard layout.Windows will now check for updates and install them as necessary.The next screen you see will be the "Sign in" screen. Click "Sign-in options" and then click "Domain join instead".For your name, use your SenecaID (ex. hheim) and click "Next".For your password, use "P@ssw0rd" and click "Next".Next, fill out 3 security questions, clicking "Next" along the way.Select "No", "No", "Required Only", "No", "No" on the next 5 screens.Windows will then do some more updates. This may take some time and the system may reboot.When it is done with updating, you will land on the Windows 11 desktop.

searchDocs.title: Part 3-2: Post-installation Tasks for Windows 11​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: Now that our Client1 is installed, there are a few things we need to do to prepare it for our labs similar to what we did on Server1 and Server2.  We will begin with the basics - time zone and computer name.  Right-click on the time in the bottom-right corner of the Windows 11 VM and left-click "Adjust date and time".Make sure the time zone is set to UTC -05:00 Eastern Time.Click the Windows icon at the bottom of the screen (4 blue squares), type "Computer Name", and then click on "View your PC name".Click "Rename this PC" and give it the name "C1-SenecaID" (for example, my Seneca ID is hheim so my Client1 computer name would be "C1-hheim").You will be asked if you want to restart the computer. Restart it.When the computer comes back up, log in and click on the Windows icon at the bottom of the screen (4 blue squares). Type "updates" and click "Check for Updates".Click the blue "Check for Updates" button in the Windows Update window.While they are downloading , scroll down and click on "Advanced Options".Turn the "Receive updates to other Microsoft products" toggle from Off to On.Click "Windows Update" at the top of the screen to get back to the main Updates window.Like on Server1, get your Client1 fully updated. This may require some time and reboots but keep updating until you are met with the "You're up to date" message.  Now that your system is fully up to date, there is one more thing we have to do. Recall that with Server1 and Server2, something called VMWare tools was automatically installed when the initial installation was complete. This will not happen on Windows 11. We will have to install it manually.  You should notice a beige bar at the bottom of your Client1 VM with a "Install Tools" button. Click that button. (If you don't see the beige bar or the button, click on "VM" in VMWare and then click on "Install VMWare Tools").Wait a few seconds and you should see a pop up in the bottom right corner of your screen that says "DVD Drive (D:) VMWare Tools". Click this pop up.A new window will pop up with a "Run setup.exe" button. Click this button. Click "Yes" when the VMware installation launcher window pops up.The VMware tools installer will start. Click "Next". Select "Typical" and click "Next". Click "Install". Click "Finish" when the installation is complete and then restart Client1.Log back into Windows and install Firefox the same way you did with Server1.Shut down Client1.  Congratulations! You now have three fully functioning virtual machines that you will be using for the rest of the course.

searchDocs.title: Investigation 1: Exploring Network information and Assigning Static IP Addresses to your Virtual Machines​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Right now, our virtual machines are all set to receive their IP addresses automatically via DHCP from the host OS. We are going to change them all to use a static IP address so that their IP address never changes.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Finding IP information on Server1​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Begin by powering on and logging in to Server1.Click the blue windows icon at the bottom of the screen, type "cmd", and press "Enter". A Windows Command Prompt window will appear.Type in "ipconfig" and press "Enter". Notice the IPv4 Address, Subnet Mask, and Default Gateway fields. What does this information tell us?Now enter "ipconfig /all". Notice that we are given a lot more information. So what are we looking for?  There are several pieces of information here that are useful to us. The result of the first command we ran gives us the IP address and its subnet mask, as well as the default gateway (or the router/device it looks to in order to send data outside of the local network.  The second command gives us more details about the networking information associate with this machine. Specifically for us, we are interested in the DHCP information and the DNS information.  The DNS server is the server that is providing translations for IP addresses to Fully Qualified Domain Names and vice versa. We will be creating our own DNS server later on in this lab.  The DHCP server is the server that is providing this machine with an IP address. When a computer with DHCP enabled comes online, it reaches out to the network via a broadcast to find a DHCP server. If it finds one, the two machines perform a DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) exchange and the DHCP server assigns an IP address to the machine that has just come online. The computer will keep this IP address for as long as it has a lease for it. You can also find the lease information in the output that we got from the "ipconfig /all" command. Using the two lease time stamps provided, we can determine how long the DHCP server has leased this IP to this machine. When we are done with part 1 here, we will change this machine to use a static IP address instead of a DHCP assigned one.  Take a look at the "Lease Obtained" and "Lease Expires" lines in the output of "ipconfig /all". Now enter "ipconfig /release". What happened?Run "ipconfig /all" again and take a look at the "Lease Obtained" line. What changed?Next, run "ipconfig /renew". What happened?Run "ipconfig /all" again and take a look at the "Lease Obtained" line. What happened?  The "ipconfig /release" and "ipconfig /renew" commands do similar things. The "/release" option releases the DHCP assigned IP address from the machine. The "/renew" option does the same thing but then also immediately asks for a new one. So why did Server1 still have a DHCP IP address when we ran "ipconfig /all" after running "ipconfig /release"?. The short answer is: VMware. There are many small factors that differ between actual physical networks and virtual networks and this is one of them. You will discover several others as you proceed through this program.  Either way, it is important to remember the distinction between those two commands.  Keep in mind that right now, VMware is effectively acting as the default gateway, DNS server, and DHCP server. Due to the virtual nature of our network, VMware and the host OS control all of these networking services (again, another intricacy of a virtual network).  Now let's do some basic network testing.  Enter "ping google.com" into the command prompt. You should see 4 replies appear. This tells you that your Server1 machine was able to contact the website "google.com" (probably hosted on a 142.x.x.x IP address). Pings are a useful tool to test network connectivity to devices that are on both our internal network and networks external to our own.Try the following 3 commands:  ping localhost ping loopback ping 127.0.0.1   What were the outputs of these commands? What were you pinging?  The loopback address (referenced as 127.0.0.1 or localhost or loopback) is a special IP address that is on all systems. It represents the system that is running it so when you ping it you are having Server1 ping itself. This may not sound super useful (and with pings it isn't) but it is very useful when testing network services that the server is providing. We will be using it later in this lab.  Now try inputting "ping -n 10 google.com". What changed about the ping output? There are times when network stability cannot be guaranteed or ascertained. So you may send out a ping and the first 4 pings fail but later pings may succeed. This is not typical but there are times when running extended pings can be useful.Finally, try inputting "ping -t google.com". What happened? How many pings are used? Press Ctrl+C when you get tired of watching pings.  Now that you have a general idea of how to get basic network information, we are going to change our network a little so that we have better control over it and so that we can begin to work with network services.

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Addressing Server1​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Minimize your command prompt window.Click the blue windows icon at the bottom of the screen, type "control panel", and press "Enter".In the top-right of the Control Panel window, change from "Category" view to "Large Icons".Click on "Network and Sharing Center".Click "Change adapter settings" on the left hand side of the window.You will see one adapter labeled "Ethernet". Double-click it.Click "Properties" in the window that appears.Double-click "Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4)".Click the "Use the following IP address: button and fill in the three fields as such: IP address: 10.10.xxx.10 (replace xxx with your dedicated number) Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0 Default Gateway: Leave BlankClick the "Use the following DNS server addresses" button and fill in the two fields as such: Preferred DNS server: 10.10.xxx.10 (replace xxx with your dedicated number) Alternate DNS server: Leave BlankClick "OK", then click "OK" again, then click "Close".Bring up your command prompt and use "ipconfig" to confirm that the correct IP address and subnet mask are assigned to Server1.  Screenshot 1: Take a screenshot of your Server1 command prompt showing the the correct IP address and subnet mask  Shut down Server1.

searchDocs.title: Part 3: Addressing Server2​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Next, we will change the IP information on Server2. This is actually easier than Server1 because we will be using Powershell.  Power on and log into Server2Enter "15" to go into the Powershell command line.Enter the following commands:  Note - Be careful with these commands. Typos will cause problems. Double check your commands before running them.Note - Your network adapter may not be named "Ethernet0" the output of the "Get-NetAdapter" command will tell you your adapter name.Note - Replace "xxx" with your assigned number.  Get-NetAdapter Set-NetIPInterface -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0" -Dhcp Disabled Get-NetIPAddress -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0" -AddressFamily IPv4 | Remove-NetIPAddress -Confirm:$false New-NetIPAddress -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0" -IPAddress 10.10.xxx.20 -PrefixLength 24   Reboot Server2.When it comes back up log in, go back to the command line, and run "ipconfig" to confirm your IP settings have saved.  Screenshot 2: Take a screenshot of your Server2 command prompt showing the the correct IP address and subnet mask  Shut down Server2.

searchDocs.title: Part 3: Addressing Client1​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Power on and log in to Client1.Using the same instructions you used for Server1, give Client1 the following configurations: IP address: 10.10.xxx.100 Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0 Default gateway: Leave Blank Preferred DNS Server: 10.10.xxx.10 (replace xxx with your dedicated number) Alternate DNS Server: Leave BlankOpen the command prompt and run "ipconfig"  Screenshot 3: Take a screenshot of your Client1 command prompt showing the the correct IP address and subnet mask  Power off Client1

searchDocs.title: Investigation 2: Windows Firewall and Packet Filtering​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Earlier in this lab, you used pings from Server1 to test connectivity with the outside world. However, that was when the IP addressed was still being assigned by DHCP. Let's see what happens now that we have statically assigned an IP address to our VMs.  Power on Server1, log in, and bring up the command prompt.Confirm that your IP address and subnet mask are still 10.10.xxx.10 and 255.255.255.0.If they are, try pinging google.  ping google.com   Your ping should fail (likely with a "request could not find..." error).  The primary reason is that Server1 does not have a default gateway. We intentionally left that configuration blank. Because of this, Server1 does not know where to send data if the target is not on its local network. Server1, Server2, and Client1 have all been configured in such a way that they can no longer connect with the Internet or anything external to their local network. However, they can still connect to each other. Let's try that next.  Power on Server2.Log in and navigate to the Powershell command line.Confirm that your IP address and subnet mask are still 10.10.xxx.20 and 255.255.255.0.

searchDocs.content: This week's lab will cover the following:  Adding and removing roles in Windows ServerLearning about and editing the registry

searchDocs.title: Lab 3 Notes​
searchDocs.content: You will be asked to take screenshots along the way in this lab. It is easier to do so rather than having to go back at the end of the lab to take them. Also, one screenshot cannot be taken once the lab has been completed so please take care to take your screenshots when instructed to.

searchDocs.title: Objectives​
searchDocs.content: By the end of this lab, you will be able to:  Add roles in Windows ServerRemove roles in Windows ServerExport Registry entries for backupAdd registry entriesmodify registry entries

searchDocs.title: Investigation 1: Installing and Removing Roles with a GUI​
Part 1: Installing Roles in Server Manager​
searchDocs.content: In this investigation, you will install 3 new roles into Server1 and then remove 1.  Begin by logging into Server1 and open Server Manager.Click on "Add roles and features".The "Add Roles and Features" wizard window will appear. Click "Next".Select "Role based or feature-based installation" and click "Next".Select your server (it should be the only one there) and click "Next".The next screen will have a listing of all he available roles that can be installed onto your Windows Server. Check the following 3 roles (NOTE: As you select each role, it will prompt you to add necessary features for that role. Accept what it gives you to install and click "Add Features"):  Print and Document ServicesWeb Server (IIS)DNS (When selecting DNS you will get a Validation Results warning. Do not worry about this. We will be fixing this issue in lab 4. Just click "Continue" when it appears)  With all 3 roles selected, click "Next".Click "Next" on the next few windows, accepting the default options each one gives you until you arrive on the "Confirm installation selections" window.Check the "Restart the destination server automatically if required" box and then click "Install".Your roles will now be installed onto Windows Server. Wait for the installations to all complete and then click "Close".  You should now see the new roles you installed have been added as tiles in your Server Manager listed under "Roles and Server Groups". They will also appear in the top-left area of Server Manager listed under "Dashboard", "Local Server", and "All Servers".  You will also notice that these tiles are all coloured red. This is because they have not been finalized because we have not rebooted.  Reboot your Server1.  When the server and Server Manager come back up, wait a moment and you will see your new Roles appear as tiles once again but now with green accents to show they are ready to go. We will leave them for now but we will come back to DNS and IIS in lab 4.  Screenshot 1: Take a screenshot showing the role tiles in Server Manager (DNS, IIS, Print Services)

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Removing Roles in Server Manager​
searchDocs.content: Now that we have roles installed let's look at how we can remove them.  In the top-right area of Server Manager, click on "Manage" >> "Remove Roles and Features".Click "Next" in the "Remove Roles and Features" wizard window.Select your server (it should be the only one there) and click "Next".Uncheck "Print and Document Services", click "Remove Features" in the window that appears, and then click "Next".Click "Next" again and then on the "Confirm removal selections" screen heck the "Restart the destination server automatically if required" box and then click "Remove".Windows will remove the Print Services role. Click "Close" when it is finished.Shut down Server1.  Screenshot 2: Take a screenshot showing the role tiles in Server Manager (DNS and IIS)  Now you know how to add and remove roles in Windows Server. Pretty easy, right? Well that's because we have the GUI to use on Server1. Next we will do the same thing on Server 2 with no GUI...

searchDocs.title: Investigation 2: Installing and Removing Roles on Server Core (with no GUI)​
Part 1: Installing Roles in Powershell​
searchDocs.content: Installing and removing roles on Server Core is not difficult but it requires the installation of the Server Manager module and the use of Powershell. We will be discussing Powershell in more detail in lab 6 and 7 but for now just keep in mind that it is required for most tasks in Server Core.  Power on and log into Server2. You should be met with the "Welcome to Windows Server 2025 Datacenter" screen with 15 options.Type "15" and press "Enter". This will bring you to the command line. Windows Server 2025 will default to a Powershell command line. You can tell because you will see the letters "PS" next to your current directory path.To install Server Manager, enter the following command:  import-module servermanager   You should see no output if it runs successfully.  Now, let's see what roles and features are already installed and which ones are available to install. Run the following command:  get-windowsfeature   This will generate a large listing of all available windows roles and features. An "X" beside a role or feature indicates that it is already installed.  Let's add a new one - the "Print Services" role.  Enter the following command:  add-windowsfeature print-services -restart   Server Core will install the Print Services role and when it has completed you will be met with output specifying the success of the installation (Exit Code: Success).  You can also confirm that the role was succussfully installed by running the "get-windowsfeature" command again. Notice that there is not an "X" next to "Print and Document Services" and "Print Server".  Screenshot 3: Take a screenshot here to show you successfully installed the Print Services role on Server2.  Now we will remove that same role.

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Removing Roles in Powershell​
searchDocs.content: Reboot your Server2 with the following command:  shutdown /r /t 0   When it is finished rebooting, log in and return to the Powershell command line. Now, enter the following command:  remove-windowsfeature print-services -restart   Windows should reboot once the role has been removed. If not, reboot manually.  Log back in, return to the Powershell command line and enter the "get-windowsfeature" command once again. Note that "X"s next to "Print and Document Services" and "Print Server" have been removed.  Screenshot 4: Take a screenshot here to show you successfully removed the Print Services role on Server2.  Shut down your Server2 with the following command:  shutdown /s /t 0

searchDocs.title: Investigation 3: The Windows Registry​
searchDocs.content: The Windows Registry is a critically important part of any Microsoft Windows operating system. It is essentially a database that stores all computer, system, application and user settings. More importantly, it is referenced by Windows for just about every operation that can occur on the OS. It cannot be overstated just how important the Registry is and how important it is to not mess around in it.  In this next section we are going to mess around in the Registry.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Exporting Registry Keys​
searchDocs.content: Before we go in and start changing things, we are going to learn how to backup up parts of the registry. We are not going to change anything critical in the Registry but (as is the case with any configuration on any system) it is always a good idea to backup your default settings. That way, if you break something, you can always revert to the backup.  Entries in the registry are called "Keys". They vary widely in structure and function but they can all be backed up the same way. We are going to be modifying the key that controls the legal notice when logging into Windows so we are going to back up that key along with the entire location in which it sits.  Power on Server1 and log in.Click the blue Windows button at the bottom of the screen and type "run" and hit "Enter".The "Run" dialogue box will appear. Enter "regedit" and click "OK". The Registry Editor window will appear. Note: Take extra care when navigating the Registry. There are many directories that appear as duplicates down different paths of the registry directory tree and you want to make sure you are in the right place before making any changes. Changes made in the wrong place can end in disastrous results.Navigate to the following path in the Registry Editor: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ SOFTWARE\ Microsoft\ Windows\ CurrentVersion\ policies\ systemIf you are in the right place you will see the "legalnoticecaption" and "legalnoticetext" keys. Click "File" in the top-left of the Registry Editor window and then click "Export".Name your backup "RegistryLegalNotice.reg" and save it to the C: drive.Using the File Explorer, navigate to your C: drive.  Screenshot 5: Take a screenshot showing your RegistryLegalNotice.reg file in the C: drive directory.

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Modifying Registry Keys​
searchDocs.content: Now that we have a backup, we can proceed to modify the legal keys.  Back in the Registry Editor, double click on the legalnoticecaption key. Enter the value as "This is a Secure PC" and click "OK".Double click on the legalnoticetext key. Enter the value as "Only authorized users can log into this computer and use this network. Non-authorized users will be recorded and prosecuted." and click "OK".Click "View" at the top of the editor and then "Refresh".Close the Registry Editor and reboot Server1.  Once it reboots and you go to log in, notice that you will now see your legal messages.  Screenshot 6: Take a screenshot showing these messages before you log in.

searchDocs.title: Part 3: Adding Registry Keys​
searchDocs.content: Keys can be modified but we can also add keys for new functionality or if keys are missing.  Log back into Server1 and open the Registry Editor again.Navigate to the following path (BE CAREFUL and double check where you are!): HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ SOFTWARE\ Microsoft\ Windows NT\ CurrentVersionIf you are in the right place you will see the several keys with "Build" in the name at the top of the list.Right-click in the white space where the keys are stored and click "New">>"String Value".Name it "RegisteredOwner",press "Enter", then double click it and enter your name for its value.Again, right-click in the white space where the keys are stored and click "New">>"String Value".Name it "RegisteredOrganization",press "Enter", then double click it and enter "Seneca Polytechnic" for its value.Click "View" at the top of the editor and then "Refresh".Hit Winkey+R on your keyboard (a nice shortcut to bring up the "Run" dialogue box). Enter "winver.exe" and click "OK". The "About Windows" window should appear and your Name and Organization will be listed at the bottom.  Screenshot 7: Take a screenshot showing your name and organization in the "About Windows" window.  Let's add another key. This time we will add something that is actually useful on our system.  Navigate to the following path in the Registry Editor (CAUTION! THIS IS A DIFFERENT PATH THAN THE LAST ONE!): HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ SOFTWARE\ Policies\ Microsoft\ Windows NTThere should be only one key here (the Default key). Right-click in the white space and click "New">>"Key". You will see a new path entry on the left side of the screen appear inside "Windows NT".Rename it to "Reliability"Now, highlight "Reliability", right-click in the white space to the right and click "New">>"DWORD".Rename it to "ShutdownReasonOn".Click "View" at the top of the editor and then "Refresh".Close the Registry Editor and reboot Server1. Notice that when you reboot Server1 you are no longer asked to provide a reason as to why the server is shutting down. But why exactly did that happen?Log back into Server1 and navigate back to your "ShutdownReasonOn" key. Double-click it and notice its "value" data. It is set to "0". You will learn about binary and hex and decimal values in another course but that "0" value means that the key is turned off. So we added a key that specifies to turn off the functionality that asks the user why they are shutting down the server. If we were to change that value to "1" we would turn that key on and the server would once again begin asking the user for reasons when shutting down.  Screenshot 8: Take a screenshot showing your ShutdownReasonOn key and its value data.
